read: partial: main text pp.1-9 (abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, dataset construction, controlled variants, experiments, conclusion, limitations) in full; appendices A-F (pp.13-19) and G.1 with Table 2 (pp.23-24) read; the scoring examples (F.3) and G.2-G.5 skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2509.17677v2, 2 May 2026 (p.1); no venue named; an ACL Code of Ethics statement (p.13) and a Limitations section (p.9) suggest an ACL-venue submission
what_it_is: EngiBench is a hierarchical benchmark of engineering problem solving at three levels: foundational knowledge retrieval, contextual reasoning and open-ended modelling (pp.1, 4). Levels 1-2 are closed-form problems filtered for engineering relevance from existing benchmarks (SuperGPQA, MMLU, MATH, GSM8k, Orca-Math, HARP, Omni-MATH, Big-Math) and university materials (pp.5, 13-14); Level 3 is 43 open-ended problems from modelling competitions with official rubrics (p.5). Each Level 1-2 problem also has LLM-written perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants; Level 3 has only a perturbed one (pp.5, 15). Levels 1-2 are scored correct or incorrect against reference answers by two LLM evaluators with a 2% numeric tolerance; Level 3 is scored by the same LLMs against expert-refined rubrics, and the scores are calibrated by human annotators (pp.6, 18-19). Sixteen LLMs were evaluated zero-shot (p.6).
domain: engineering: Systems & Control, Physical & Structural, and Chemical & Biological subfields (p.5), drawn from disciplines such as electrical, mechanical, civil, chemical and biomedical engineering (pp.2, 14)
size: 939 + 354 + 467 problems across the three subfields (p.5), 1,760 by my sum, of which 43 are Level 3 (p.5); each Level 1-2 problem has three variants (p.5); 16 LLMs (p.6)
source_of_items: Levels 1-2: existing public benchmarks and university course materials, filtered and classified by an LLM pipeline with human verification (pp.5, 13-14); Level 3: modelling competitions (CUMCM, MCM/ICM, APMCM, 2010-2024), translated and paraphrased by LLM under expert supervision (pp.14-15); variants: LLM-written and manually verified (p.15)
instances: perturbed: static items, each with one LLM-written perturbed variant (changed numbers and/or wording) plus knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction rewrites for Levels 1-2 (pp.5, 15-17)
has_gold_traces: no for Levels 1-2: the released fields hold reference answers only (pp.17-18), although the perturbation prompt asks the LLM for a rewritten step-by-step solution (p.16). Level 3 tasks come with reference solutions from top-ranking competition entries (p.5), which are used for the human scores, not as step references.
evaluation: Levels 1-2: final answer, binary, judged by GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash against the reference answer with a +/-2% numeric tolerance; disagreements are resolved by hand (p.18). Level 3: rubric scoring (0-10 per capability dimension) by the same two LLMs, averaged, then reviewed and calibrated by annotators with engineering backgrounds (pp.6, 19)
human_validation: The Level 1-2 evaluators were checked on 300 randomly sampled, manually verified problems: 98.67% accuracy for GPT-4.1 and 98.33% for Gemini 2.5 Flash (p.18). Level 3 problems and rubrics were reviewed by 20 PhD students and engineering professionals (p.5); the rubrics were drafted by an LLM from official contest standards, cross-checked by two reviewers with engineering backgrounds and adjudicated by prize-winning modelling-competition experts (pp.18-19). Level 3 LLM scores were calibrated by annotators, and human-calibrated, LLM-only and human-only averages are close (Table 2, pp.23-24). No inter-rater agreement statistic is reported.
contamination_measures: perturbations: the perturbed variants 'reduce possible overlap with pretraining data' (p.5) and Level 3 tasks are paraphrased by LLM 'to minimize potential overlap with pretraining data' (p.15); accuracy drops under perturbation are reported, e.g. on Level 2: -9.3% for GPT-4.1 Nano, -11.4% for Qwen2.5-7B, -8.3% for Mixtral-8x7B (p.7); the data are public on GitHub (p.1)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' S-I3c (L116-122): 'unlike existing benchmarks (e.g., Zhou et al., 2025; Mudur et al., 2025) that rely solely on outcome matching, demand holistic procedural reasoning'. Also covered by S-E3 (L199-205): 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning required for engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: The overall verdict is the worst of the three. Each May sentence describes one part of EngiBench as if it were the whole, and the two contradict each other (citation map C6). S-E2, misleading: only Level 3, 43 problems (p.5), is rubric-scored. Levels 1-2, the great majority of the 939 + 354 + 467 problems (p.5), are scored by binary final-answer checks against reference answers (p.18), so the sentence omits what matters most for EngTrace's comparison: most of EngiBench is outcome-matched. 'Subjective' is the May paper's word, not supported by the paper. Its rubrics are built from official contest scoring standards, cross-checked by two reviewers and adjudicated by experts (pp.18-19). The LLM scores are human-calibrated, and LLM-only, calibrated and human-only averages are close (Table 2, p.24), though no agreement statistic is given. S-I3c, wrong: Level 3 scores open-ended solutions against rubrics on four capability dimensions (pp.6, 8, 19), so EngiBench does not rely 'solely on outcome matching'. S-E3, misleading for this paper: Levels 1-2 are outcome-matched, but Level 3 assesses the reasoning shown in an open-ended solution, including domain-specific reasoning (Fig. 5b, p.8), by rubric. What EngiBench lacks is a gold step-level reference and a verifiable check of intermediate steps, not every form of assessment beyond the outcome.

suggested_wording: EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) spans three engineering subfields at three levels of difficulty, scoring closed-form problems, filtered from existing benchmarks and course materials and rewritten into perturbed and simplified variants, by final answer, and 43 open-ended modelling-competition tasks by LLM judges against expert-refined rubrics with human calibration; no level checks intermediate steps against a reference solution.
facts_to_cite: Three difficulty levels: foundational knowledge retrieval, contextual reasoning and open-ended modelling (pp.1, 4)
Three subfields: Systems & Control (939 problems), Physical & Structural (354) and Chemical & Biological (467) (p.5)
Level 1-2 problems are filtered for engineering relevance from existing benchmarks (including SuperGPQA, MMLU, MATH and GSM8k) and from university materials (pp.5, 13-14)
Level 3 has 43 open-ended problems from modelling competitions with official scoring rubrics, reviewed by 20 PhD students and engineering professionals (p.5)
Each Level 1-2 problem is rewritten by an LLM into perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants, which are manually verified; Level 3 has only a perturbed variant (pp.5, 15)

Levels 1-2 are scored correct or incorrect against reference answers by GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash with a 2% numeric tolerance; on 300 manually verified problems the two evaluators are 98.67% and 98.33% accurate (p.18)

Level 3 is scored by the same two LLMs against expert-refined rubrics on four capability dimensions (information extraction, domain-specific reasoning, multi-objective decision-making, uncertainty handling), averaged and then calibrated by human annotators (pp.6, 19)
Sixteen LLMs evaluated zero-shot; accuracy falls from Level 1 to Level 2, and on Level 3 every model scores below the human expert average of 8.74 (pp.6-7)
Perturbed variants lower Level 2 accuracy, e.g. by 9.3% for GPT-4.1 Nano and 11.4% for Qwen2.5-7B; most models score highest on the math-abstraction variant (pp.7-8)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: a multi-subfield engineering scope with difficulty tiers; a contamination probe by LLM-written rewrites (EngiBench's perturbed variant changes numbers and wording, pp.15-16, while EngTrace's paraphrase arm keeps the numbers); human checks of the evaluator (300 sampled answers; the Level 3 score comparison); experts in rubric construction. Lacks: template generation (its variants are single LLM rewrites of existing, mostly public items, not parameterised templates); gold reasoning traces; step-level evaluation of any kind against a reference; a deterministic checker (even Levels 1-2 are judged by LLMs, whose prompt asks them to check 'core calculation steps' but return only True or False, p.18); a private test set (the data are public); agreement statistics for the rubric scoring.
notes: Version: the text is v2 (2 May 2026); the May submission may have read v1 (September 2025), which I could not see, so details may differ from what its authors read. '1,760' is my sum of the three subfield counts; I did not find the total stated in the text. A surprise for Batch E1: EngiBench's reference list has 'Yuheng Cheng, Huan Zhao, Xiyuan Zhou, Junhua Zhao, Yuji Cao, Chao Yang, and Xinlei Cai. 2025. A large language model for advanced power dispatch. Scientific Reports, 15(1):8925' (p.10), and lists ElecBench separately and correctly as Xiyuan Zhou, Huan Zhao, Yuheng Cheng et al. 2024, arXiv:2407.05365 (p.12). The May 'Cheng et al., 2024' ElecBench entry (May text L921-925) prints exactly the first of these author lists with ElecBench's title and id, which suggests the two entries were merged; this explains the wrong first author found in citation map C-S. The note in the May entry naming 'EngiBench by Felten et al.' is reviewed under felten2025engibench.
